title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
hookLine: Ganesha eats Kubera's whole feast and stays hungry, until one handful given with love fills him
carry: ganesha counts the love, not the feast
last: NO TYRANT CAN HOLD GOD'S POWER.

cards: A story told in many homes at Ganesh Chaturthi. Kubera, the god of wealth, wants everyone to see how rich he is, so he invites Shiva to a feast. Shiva sends his son instead: Ganesha, small and round.
Kubera serves him course after course, and Ganesha eats it all. Then the rest of the kitchen. Then, the story says, the furniture, and he's still hungry.
Kubera runs to Shiva in a panic. And the boy's parents give him one small handful of food, offered with love. Ganesha eats it, and he's full.

teach.b: That story is the key to Ganesh Chaturthi, a festival kept for a day and a half, or five, seven or ten days. Families invite Ganesha in as a guest of honor and feed him modaks, sweets, fruit, flowers.
Not because God needs a meal; Kubera's whole palace couldn't fill him.

teach.h: BHAVA: THE LOVE BEHIND THE OFFERING.
teach.b: What fills him is bhava, the love behind the offering. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the same: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept.
It's one of the plainest teachings in Hinduism: God counts the love, not the size of the plate. Then comes the last day, Anant Chaturdashi.

teach.h: FOOD FOR THE ROAD, AND FORGIVENESS.
teach.b: Before the image leaves home, the family gathers for a final aarti, offers food for the road, often curd rice or modaks, and asks forgiveness for anything they did wrong as hosts.
At the water, the crowd shouts one call, in Marathi: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Ganpati, our dear father, Morya: next year, come early. Bappa is an affectionate word, like dad.

teach.h: GANESHA COUNTS THE LOVE, NOT THE FEAST.
teach.b: Morya is often linked to Morya Gosavi, a Ganesha saint remembered at Chinchwad near Pune. Then the image is carried in and slowly let go: visarjan, a word whose root sense is closer to releasing.
People cry, grown men too. But the guest has been loved, fed and thanked, and the last word isn't goodbye. It's come back soon.

how: On the last day of Ganesh Chaturthi, often Anant Chaturdashi, families perform a final aarti, offer food for the journey, ask forgiveness for any lapse as hosts, and carry the image to water, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya.

o: a harvest festival when new rice is cooked in pots
Ganesha's festival: welcomed home, then let go in water
a spring festival when bonfires are lit at night

games.q: the guest who's filled by love — tap the pairs.
p: the god of wealth who throws the feast

s: he eats it all and stays hungry; one handful given with love fills him.
families ask Ganesha's forgiveness before the immersion
for anything they did wrong as hosts during his stay.
the farewell cry means goodbye forever
pudhchya varshi lavkar ya: next year, come early.

games.q: your family can't do a big Ganesha or a fancy spread this year. by Kubera's story, what matters?
o: a small image and a little food, offered with real love.
skip the festival until you can do it properly.
borrow money to match the neighbors.
games.why: Kubera's palace couldn't fill Ganesha; one handful given with love did. what counts is the bhava, the love behind it.

practice: Many Hindus offer food to God before they eat it, then receive it back as prasad. Take one small thing: a sip of water, a flower, a piece of fruit.
If you pray, hold it up for Ganesha, or for God as you know God, and offer it with your whole heart. If you don't pray, offer it in your mind to someone you love, and mean it.
Then, on an out-breath, say what the crowd says: come back soon.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. Up to ten days of feeding a guest who is filled by love, ending with visarjan and the cry Ganpati Bappa Morya: come back soon.

orig.note: Marathi: Ganpati, dear father, Morya. the cry continues: pudhchya varshi lavkar ya, come early next year.

carryVoice: Your line: ganesha counts the love, not the feast. One handful was enough. Until tomorrow.
